title: Karya Learn
about: Karya's data annotators are some of the most overworked and underpaid workers in India — but the same digital work that pays them can also teach them something, if it's designed to. I led Karya Learn to test that idea, starting with financial literacy: a nine-chapter, story-based curriculum written in the Sabido method — the same dramatized-storytelling technique long used to teach family planning and public health through soap operas — delivered chapter by chapter on a WhatsApp-style interface, and read aloud by workers as paid data-collection work in its own right.

process.title: Learning and earning were a trade-off
process.text: Rural and semi-urban gig workers doing India's growing data-annotation work had no built-in way to build skills while they earned — the work paid, but it didn't teach anything back.

process.title: A story people could see themselves in
process.text: 55 participants (42 women, 13 men) from a stone quarry worker community in Wagholi, Pune — most earning under ₹15,000/month, many without active bank accounts — read aloud and recorded a 9-module financial literacy curriculum built around a relatable protagonist, so the same paid task doubled as both a lesson and a source of usable speech data.

process.title: Learning, and good data, at once
process.text: Comprehension scores rose from 18.01 to 23.31 out of 27 (p<0.0001, Cohen's d=1.32), 85% of the ~80 hours of recorded speech was rated good-quality data, and several participants reported real behaviour change afterward — trying UPI for the first time, or starting to save small amounts of money.
